summary: Specifies version 2 of Multicast Listener Discovery, used by IPv6 routers to learn which multicast addresses neighbors want. MLDv2 lets a node ask for traffic from specific sources, or from all except some. It updates RFC 2710, was updated by RFC 4604, and was replaced by RFC 9777.

plainLanguage.summary: MLDv2 is the IPv6 version of the protocol that lets routers find out which multicast groups the machines on their network are listening to. The second version lets a machine also say which sources it wants traffic from, so a router can block the rest and save bandwidth.

questions: how does mld source filtering work
what is the difference between mldv1 and mldv2
subtitle: How an IPv6 router learns which multicast groups its neighbours listen to, and which sources they want.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 router has to know which multicast addresses its neighbouring hosts are listening to, so that it forwards traffic only where someone wants it, and MLDv1 could not say anything about the sources a host wanted.
tldr.mechanism: MLDv2 adds source filtering: a host reports that it wants a group from particular sources, or from every source but a few. The router summarises what it hears into an INCLUDE or EXCLUDE mode with a source list, and a querier polls the link to refresh the state.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is interoperable with MLDv1 and specifies the message formats, the timers and the state machines. The RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 9777, and it was later updated by RFC 4604.

today: RFC 3810 is a June 2004 standards-track specification of MLDv2, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 9777. It was later updated by RFC 4604.

sections.title: What MLD Does and What MLDv2 Adds
sections.content:
The Multicast Listener Discovery Protocol is used by IPv6 routers to discover the presence of multicast listeners, that is nodes that wish to receive multicast packets, on their directly attached links, and to discover specifically which multicast addresses are of interest to those neighbouring nodes. A multicast router may itself be a listener, in which case it performs both the router part and the listener part of the protocol, so that it can collect the information its multicast routing protocol needs and inform itself and its neighbouring routers of its own listening state.

The previous version of MLD is specified in RFC 2710 and is called MLDv1 in this document. MLDv2 is a translation of the IGMPv3 protocol for IPv6 semantics. Compared with MLDv1, MLDv2 adds support for source filtering, which is the ability for a node to report interest in listening to packets only from specific source addresses, as required to support source-specific multicast, or from all but specific source addresses sent to a particular multicast address. MLDv2 is designed to be interoperable with MLDv1.

The protocol is asymmetric. It specifies separate behaviour for multicast address listeners and for multicast routers. The purpose of MLD is to enable each multicast router to learn, for each of its directly attached links, which multicast addresses and which sources have interested listeners on that link, and that information is handed to whichever multicast routing protocol the router uses, so that packets reach the links where listeners are waiting.

A router only needs to know that at least one node on an attached link is listening to a given address from a given source; it is not required to keep track of each neighbouring node's interests separately. If several multicast routers sit on the same subnet, a querier election mechanism elects a single router to be in Querier state. All the routers on the subnet listen to the messages sent by listeners and maintain the same listening state, so any of them can take over the querier role if the current one fails, but only the querier sends the periodic and triggered query messages.
sections.plainLanguage: MLD answers one question for the router: is anyone on this link listening to this group? The second version lets the answer be more precise, so it can also say which senders the listeners want to hear from.

sections.title: The Two Filter Modes
sections.content:
Upper-layer protocols and applications on a listening node use service interface calls to ask the IP layer to enable or disable reception of packets sent to specific multicast addresses. The node keeps multicast address listening state for each socket on which those calls have been made. In addition to this per-socket state, a node must maintain or compute listening state for each of its interfaces.

Conceptually, that per-interface state consists of a set of records, each holding an IPv6 multicast address, a filter mode and a source list. The filter mode is either INCLUDE or EXCLUDE. In INCLUDE mode, reception of packets sent to the specified multicast address is enabled only from the source addresses listed in the source list. In EXCLUDE mode, reception is enabled from all source addresses except those listed in the source list.

At most one record exists per multicast address for a given interface. This per-interface state is derived from the per-socket state, but may differ from it when different sockets have different filter modes or source lists for the same multicast address and interface. After a multicast packet has been accepted from an interface by the IP layer, its delivery to the application on a particular socket depends on the listening state of that socket, and possibly on other conditions such as the transport-layer port the socket is bound to. MLDv2 messages are not themselves subject to source filtering and must always be processed by hosts and routers.
sections.plainLanguage: A node can say either of two things about a group: I want these senders, or I want everyone except these. The node keeps one list per interface, whatever its programs asked for, and a router uses that list to decide what to forward.

sections.title: Queries and Reports Between the Querier and the Listeners
sections.content:
There are three types of query message. General Queries are sent periodically by the querier to learn listener information from an attached link, and they build and refresh the multicast address listener state inside all the routers on the link. Multicast Address Specific Queries ask about one multicast address, and Multicast Address and Source Specific Queries ask about a set of sources for one address.

Nodes answer queries by reporting their per-interface listening state in Current State Report messages, sent to a multicast address that all the MLDv2 routers on the link listen to. When a node's listening state changes, it reports the change immediately in a State Change Report, which carries either filter mode change records, source list change records, or both.

State changes are mainly triggered by the expiration of a timer or by the arrival of an MLD message, and a service interface call can also trigger a listener state change. To make the protocol robust in spite of unreliable message exchange, messages are retransmitted several times, and timers are set to allow for message loss and for the retransmissions. Periodical General Queries and Current State Reports are not retransmitted in this way, to avoid overloading the link; they exist to refresh state, so a lost one is caught by the next reporting period.

The number of retransmissions depends on the Robustness Variable, which lets the protocol be tuned to the expected packet loss on a link. MLD is robust to a number of packet losses equal to the Robustness Variable minus one, and the document recommends a default value of 2. The relevant timers have default values too: the Query Interval, the interval between General Queries, defaults to 125 seconds, and the Query Response Interval, the Maximum Response Delay inserted into the periodic General Queries, defaults to 10000, which is 10 seconds.

When a node says through a State Change Report that it wants to stop listening to a particular address or source, the querier must query for other listeners of that address or source before deleting it from its state and stopping the traffic. Both the address-specific and the address-and-source-specific queries are sent only in response to State Change Reports, never in response to Current State Reports, so that the router does not treat every report as a possible state change.
sections.plainLanguage: The querier asks the link who is listening, and the machines answer. A machine also says so when its own listening changes. Because messages can be lost, everything is sent more than once, and the number of retries is set by a robustness value that you can raise on a lossy link.

sections.title: What a Router Keeps for Each Address
sections.content:
Multicast routers that implement MLDv2, whether or not they are in querier state, keep state per multicast address per attached link. That listener state consists of a filter mode, a filter timer and a source list, with a timer associated with each source in the list. The filter mode summarises the total listening state of a multicast address into a minimum set that respects all the nodes' states, and it may change when particular reports arrive or when timer conditions occur.

A router is in INCLUDE mode for an address if all the listeners on the link interested in that address are in INCLUDE mode. The state is written as INCLUDE (A), where A is the Include List, the set of sources that one or more listeners have asked to receive. All the sources in the Include List are forwarded by the router, and any source not in it is blocked. A source is added to the Include List when a listener in INCLUDE mode reports it, and each source has a source timer that is refreshed whenever a listener confirms its interest in it. When the timer of a source expires, that source is deleted from the Include List. This is the soft leave mechanism.

The fast leave scheme is also based on the source timers. When a node in INCLUDE mode says it wants to stop listening to a specific source, the routers on the link lower their timers for that source, and the querier sends a Multicast Address and Source Specific Query to check whether anyone else wants that source. If a report including that source arrives before the timer expires, the routers update the timer; if not, the source is deleted from the Include List.

A router is in EXCLUDE mode for an address if there is at least one listener in EXCLUDE mode for that address on the link, and the state is written as EXCLUDE (X,Y), where X is the Requested List and Y is the Exclude List. All sources except those in the Exclude List are forwarded. The Requested List has no effect on forwarding, but the router maintains it for two reasons: to keep track of the sources that listeners in INCLUDE mode listen to, so that the switch back to INCLUDE mode does not interrupt the flow of traffic to them, and to allow fast blocking of previously unblocked sources, whose timers are set to a small value and checked with a source-specific query before being moved to the Exclude List and blocked.
sections.plainLanguage: A router does not keep every machine's wish list. It merges them: if every listener wants particular sources, the router forwards exactly those and blocks the rest. If at least one listener wants everything, the router forwards everything except the sources that listener asked to exclude.

sections.title: The Message Formats
sections.content:
MLDv2 is a sub-protocol of ICMPv6, so its message types are a subset of ICMPv6 messages, and the messages are identified in IPv6 packets by a preceding Next Header value of 58. All MLDv2 messages must be sent with a link-local IPv6 source address, an IPv6 Hop Limit of 1, and an IPv6 Router Alert option in a Hop-by-Hop options header, which is needed so that routers examine MLDv2 messages sent to multicast addresses in which they have no interest. Reports may be sent with the source address set to the unspecified address if a valid link-local source address has not yet been acquired for the sending interface.

Two message types concern the MLDv2 protocol: the Multicast Listener Query, type 130, and the Version 2 Multicast Listener Report, type 143. To interoperate with nodes that implement MLDv1, an implementation of MLDv2 must also support the Version 1 Multicast Listener Report, type 131, and the Version 1 Multicast Listener Done, type 132. Unrecognized message types must be silently ignored.

The Query message carries a type field, a code field, a checksum, a Maximum Response Code, a reserved field, the multicast address being queried, and a group of fields holding the S flag, the QRV, the QQIC and the number of sources, followed by the source addresses themselves. The checksum is the standard ICMPv6 checksum, covering the entire MLDv2 message plus a pseudo-header of IPv6 header fields, and it must be verified before the message is processed. The Maximum Response Code gives the maximum time allowed before a responding report is sent, in units of milliseconds, derived from the code either directly or, for larger values, as a floating-point value. The S flag, set in later copies of a query, tells receiving routers to suppress the timer updates they would normally perform on hearing a query. The QRV field carries the querier's robustness value when it is not zero, and the QQIC field carries the querier's query interval in seconds, again derived either directly or as a floating-point value.
sections.plainLanguage: The queries and reports are ICMPv6 messages, which is why they carry a checksum. They travel one hop only, from a link-local address, with the router alert option set so that routers bother to look at them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Before processing an MLD message, nodes verify that the source address of the message is a valid link-local address, or the unspecified address, that the Hop Limit is set to 1, and that the Router Alert option is present in the Hop-by-Hop options header of the IPv6 packet. If any of these checks fails, the packet is dropped, which defends the nodes from acting on forged MLD messages that originated off-link. The RFC therefore discusses only the effects of on-link forgery.

A forged Query message from a machine with a lower IPv6 address than the current querier will cause the querier duties to be assigned to the forger. If the forger then sends no more queries, the other routers' Other Querier Present timer times out and one of them resumes the role, and during that time, if the forger ignores Multicast Listener Done messages, traffic might flow to multicast addresses with no listeners for up to the Multicast Address Listener Interval. A forged Version 1 Query message will put MLDv2 listeners on that link into MLDv1 Host Compatibility Mode, and that scenario can be avoided by giving MLDv2 hosts a configuration option to ignore Version 1 messages completely. A denial of service attack on a node could be staged through forged Multicast Address and Source Specific Queries.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages that do not come from the local link are dropped by the checks on the source address, the hop limit and the router alert option. Someone on the same link can still lie, for example by pretending to be the querier, so the protocol is written to recover quickly when that happens.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Initialized to zero by the sender and ignored by receivers.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: The standard ICMPv6 checksum over the message and a pseudo-header of IPv6 fields.

fields.name: Maximum Response Code
fields.desc: The maximum time allowed before a responding report, in milliseconds.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Initialized to zero by the sender and ignored by receivers.

fields.name: Multicast Address
fields.desc: The address being queried; zero in a General Query.

fields.name: S Flag
fields.desc: Set to ask receiving routers to suppress their normal timer updates.

fields.name: QRV
fields.desc: The querier's Robustness Variable, when it is not zero.

fields.name: QQIC
fields.desc: The querier's Query Interval code, in seconds.

fields.name: Number of Sources (N)
fields.desc: How many source addresses follow; zero in a General Query.

fields.name: Source Address [i]
fields.desc: The unicast source addresses the query asks about.
